strengths: R2E offers a coherent, NLP-relevant approach to evidence-based entity ranking. Candidate-specific retrieval, a set-transformer reasoner, and training with NULL evidence make sentence-level Shapley attribution a well-defined component of the prediction pipeline.

The gene-ranking experiments demonstrate improvements even without frequency correction. For example, uncorrected R2E achieves MRR 0.202 versus 0.176 for the strongest baseline on Gene Description Facts. Updating retrieval evidence also improves performance without retraining, directly supporting the adaptability claim.

The literature evaluations use document-level separation, temporal splits, and models trained from scratch to reduce contamination. Architecture and modality ablations, detailed appendices, and the announced release of three evaluation datasets are valuable methodological contributions.

The auditing experiment provides a concrete downstream use for explanations: removing GPT-4-identified irrelevant evidence improves clinical AUROC from 0.633 to 0.638, with a reported paired significance test. The qualitative analysis usefully discusses failures of both R2E and GPT-4.
weaknesses: Reproducibility remains materially constrained despite the extensive methodological description. Training and retrieval depend on a partly proprietary corpus and proprietary entity linking, while code and model weights are explicitly withheld. Released evaluation datasets enable benchmark reuse but do not enable reproduction of the reported system. An executable reference implementation with an accessible corpus, or sufficient shared processed resources, would substantially strengthen the case for Findings.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the source of the ranking gains. Frequency correction is applied to R2E but corresponding corrected MLM results are absent, although Appendix G explicitly derives that correction. On clinical outcomes, literature-only R2E achieves 0.632 AUROC versus 0.630 for MLM; this supports comparable predictive performance with added attribution more clearly than a substantive accuracy advantage.

The clinical results contain an unresolved reporting inconsistency: Table 3 reports 0.632 AUROC for literature-only R2E-Cor, whereas Table S8 reports 0.639 for the apparently corresponding standard-training configuration. This discrepancy exceeds the reported auditing improvement. Configurations, evaluation subsets, and run variability need clarification, together with uncertainty estimates for the principal comparisons.

Temporal controls are convincing for the literature component but incomplete for the combined and audited systems. The genetics evidence comes from a 2023 resource without a described historical cutoff, and GPT-4 can introduce knowledge acquired after the evaluated trials. These experiments therefore do not establish the stated prediction setting using exclusively evidence available before the trials; this concern does not invalidate the literature-only results.

Explanation validation relies mainly on GPT-4 relevance judgments. Human validation covers only eight query-target pairs per task, with agreement of 71.5% and 82.2%; clinical Shapley-versus-GPT-4 AUROC is only 0.665. Shapley values establish attribution under the chosen masking procedure, but these results provide limited independent evidence of biological relevance. Comparisons against retrieval similarity and simpler attribution methods would also establish whether Shapley-based selection specifically benefits auditing.

The clinical benchmark measures a noisy surrogate for therapeutic efficacy: discontinued Phase II/III development is treated as failure, although commercial, safety, and molecule-specific factors can determine discontinuation. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but some conclusions still overextend to predicting efficacy and discovering promising novel targets. The supported conclusion is narrower: association with retrospective development outcomes.
